title: Beyond Feasibility: Finite-Depth Accessibility in Constrained QAOA
authors: Rushikesh Ubale, Gregory T. Byrd, Yasar Mulani, Sangram Deshpande
abstract: Constraint-preserving mixers keep QAOA within a feasible subspace, but feasibility and global mixer connectivity do not determine which feasible configurations are available to a particular shallow circuit. We study constrained QAOA at the level of the circuit actually executed: a specified feasible initial state, finite depth, and finite schedule of mixer interactions. We define the finite-depth accessible set $R_p(M,x_0)$ and show that the computational-basis support of the ideal QAOA circuit is contained within it. This gives a parameter-independent objective ceiling $f_R^\star=\max_{x\in R_p}f(x)$ and a normalized reachable-quality diagnostic $Q_R$, separating accessible volume from the objective quality contained within it.   We evaluate this framework using resource-matched block-local XY mixer schedules for constrained portfolio optimization and synthetic block-constrained quadratic problems. Across 207 favorable-tail CVaR QAOA configurations, $Q_R$ shows the strongest association with realized shallow-QAOA performance among the structural diagnostics considered, with Pearson and Spearman correlations of $0.7003$ and $0.8057$; the relationship remains positive under controlled and dependence-aware analyses. The distinction persists across changes in feasible initialization, portfolio size, and objective family.   A compilation-only study further shows that, for the dense portfolio Hamiltonians considered here, phase-separator routing dominates the compiled two-qubit resource scale, while mixer schedules with comparable compiled two-qubit cost can exhibit markedly different finite-depth accessible quality. These results motivate objective-relevant finite-depth accessibility as a complementary diagnostic for resource-bounded constrained QAOA.
summary: This work develops a diagnostic framework to measure 'finite-depth accessibility' in constrained QAOA, focusing on which solutions are structurally available given a limited circuit depth. By defining the accessible set $R_p$ and the diagnostic $Q_R$, the authors show that this structural measure correlates strongly with actual performance, offering a vital tool for resource-bounded quantum algorithm design.
main_problem: The paper investigates the structural limitations of Constrained QAOA at finite circuit depth, moving beyond simple feasibility or global connectivity analyses.
main_result: A normalized reachable-quality diagnostic ($Q_R$) shows the strongest correlation with realized shallow-QAOA performance, suggesting objective-relevant accessibility is a key metric.
method: The authors define the finite-depth accessible set $R_p(M, x_0)$ based on the executed mixer schedule and derive metrics like $Q_R$ to quantify the objective quality within this structurally accessible region.
model_or_system: The model is the Constrained Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) applied to combinatorial optimization problems with hard constraints. The evolution is governed by a fixed initial state, a finite depth $p$, and a specific schedule of mixer interactions.
key_observables: Finite-depth accessible set $R_p(M, x_0)$, best structurally accessible objective $f^\star_R$, and the normalized reachable-quality diagnostic $Q_R$.
important_parameters: Circuit depth ($p$), initial state ($x_0$), and the specific mixer schedule ($M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the structural accessibility $R_p$ provides a parameter-independent ceiling on the best objective achievable by the fixed circuit structure.
figures_summary: Figure 1 conceptually distinguishes between global feasible connectivity and finite-depth accessibility, while the text describes the structure of the portfolio benchmark.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need to study finite-depth accessibility beyond mere feasibility, to defining the set $R_p(M, x_0)$ and the diagnostic $Q_R$, and finally validating this framework using resource-matched schedules on portfolio optimization problems.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, structural diagnostic ($Q_R$) that quantifies the *opportunity* for optimization based on the actual circuit structure, which is crucial for designing resource-constrained quantum algorithms.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Conceptual distinction between global feasible con- nectivity and finite-depth accessibility. Although the full constraint-preserving mixer structure may connect the feasi- ble manifold F, a circuit initialized at x0 and executing only a finite mixer schedule can structurally access only Rp(M, x0) ⊆ F. The accessible set contains the computational-basis sup- port of the ideal circuit and defines the best reachable objec- tive f ⋆ R and normalized reachable quality QR.

FIG. 2. Disjoint-round semantics and mixer-schedule construction. (a) A single round can contain several vertex-disjoint XY exchanges, so all compatible subsets of the active exchanges contribute to the structural accessible set. (b) The fixed, rotating- disjoint, random-disjoint, and objective-improving schedule constructions used in the experiments; their precise definitions are given in Sec. III C.

FIG. 3. Canonical resource-matched QAOA performance at requested XY-interaction budgets B = 8 and B = 16. Bars show the effective QAOA score for the deterministic mixer policies and the mean score across random-disjoint schedule seeds; error bars indicate the corresponding variability where applicable. Despite matching the requested interaction budget, the mixer allocations produce substantially different shallow-QAOA performance.

FIG. 4. Cross-domain relationship between finite-depth reachable quality and realized shallow-QAOA performance. Left: effective QAOA score Seff versus best reachable normalized quality QR across the 207 completed portfolio and synthetic QAOA configurations. Right: partial Pearson associations between Seff and the structural diagnostics after controlling for problem size n, executed XY-interaction budget, and problem domain. Among the tested diagnostics, QR shows the strongest controlled association with realized performance. The associations are observational rather than causal.

FIG. 5. Compilation diagnostics for the nested portfolio circuits. (a) Two-qubit gate counts for the separately transpiled cost, mixer, and full circuits on the sparse hardware-inspired topology. (b) Full-circuit two-qubit counts for n = 20 across the three connectivity models and the two logical XY budgets. Error bars show the sample standard deviation across the retained compiled rows in each topology–budget group. (c) Best reachable normalized quality QR versus full transpiled two-qubit gate count for the connectivity-constrained cases; marker shape identifies the mixer policy and marker fill distinguishes the two- dimensional mesh from the sparse hardware-inspired topology.
